text:
### Observed differences

- In the earlier window every trace followed one backbone: A25, then the group A28/A30/A31 (in no fixed order among themselves), then the group A32/A33/A34 (also unordered internally), then A26 — each of these six activities appeared in 100% of the 200 earlier traces, exactly once per case. In the later window, A28, A30 and A31 each appear in about 47 in 100 traces and A32, A33 and A34 in about 56 in 100, while A25 and A26 still appear in every trace. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006, REL001, REL007]

- The two groups became mutually exclusive: before, any pairing across the groups (e.g., A28 with A32, A30 with A34) co-occurred in 100% of traces with the first-group activity earlier; in the later window such pairs co-occur in only about 2 in 100 traces — in about 54 in 100 only the A32-side activity runs, in about 45 in 100 only the A28-side activity, and in about 2 in 100 both. [REL015, REL017, REL019, REL021, REL022, REL024]

- Group cohesion persists: A28, A30 and A31 still always run together when they run (about 47 in 100 traces, mixed order), and A32, A33 and A34 together in about 56 in 100, likewise without a fixed order. [REL013, REL014, REL018, REL025, REL026, REL027]

- Routing changed accordingly: before, A25's outgoing transitions went only to A28, A30 or A31 (about 34%, 37% and 30%); in the later window about 54 in 100 go directly to A32, A33 or A34, which never happened earlier. A28, A30 and A31, which previously never led to A26, now do so in roughly 26–36 in 100 of their outgoing transitions. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004]

- Event-position gaps shrank in step: A25 to A32/A33/A34, and A28/A30/A31 to A26, moved from almost always 4–5 positions apart to mostly 1–3 positions apart. [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG008, LAG011]

- Screening qualified 50 control-flow items where roughly 0.6 would be expected if nothing had changed, so the volume of flagged differences itself exceeds chance. [screening]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that, in the later window, the segment composed of the group A28/A30/A31 followed by the group A32/A33/A34 became optional and split into mutually exclusive alternatives: about 45 in 100 cases run A25, the A28/A30/A31 group, then A26 directly (skipping A32/A33/A34); about 53 in 100 run A25 directly into the A32/A33/A34 group and then A26 (skipping A28/A30/A31); about 2 in 100 still run both groups. A25 and A26 remain in every case, A25 still precedes A32 and A28 still precedes A26 whenever they co-occur, and each group keeps its mixed internal order — so this is a participation change (the two groups became skippable and essentially exclusive), not a reordering or relocation of activities. [OCC001, OCC004, REL015, REL004, REL010, DIR001]

Supporting signs: the participation drops are large and measured on 200 traces per window; the routing and gap changes match the bypass (A25 now leads directly into the second group, the first group now exits to A26, gaps shrink from 4–5 to 1–3 positions); cross-group co-occurrence fell to about 2 in 100, far below the roughly 26 in 100 expected if the two groups were skipped independently, which points to exclusivity rather than two unrelated optional blocks; and 50 qualified items against about 0.6 expected by chance rules out sampling as an explanation of the pattern as a whole. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, LAG001, LAG004, LAG008, LAG011, REL015, screening]

Limitations: the evidence cannot show what governs the choice between the two alternatives, nor distinguish a single new decision point after A25 from two independently optional groups; several indicators describe the same traces, so their agreement is not independent confirmation; and a few gap items (e.g., A28–A32, A30–A34) rest on only about 4 after-window observations and were not relied upon. [REL015, LAG005, LAG010]
